content:
This is more of a meta thread , so if inappropriate feel free to delete.

I am simply and earnestly curious as to the thought process of some new members , in terms of “rushing “ to be a Mathlib contributor . What is the reason this is actually so vaunted ?

I get that it’s a high star , official repo , but at the same time in such a niche I struggle to see the pragmatic benefit , esp with code the author themselves does not understand at all ( and almost all of these do not make it , why not look at the closed ones and see why first ?).

This sounds a bit hostile but it really really is not , I am genuinely curious , and I have often DMed specific new people just trying to ask what their Lean journey was like, why Mathlib and how did they get there.

I've been contributing to mathlib(3) since 2022 so I'm not a new member, but my rationale is simply that I like clean code, I want to publish some of my code akin to traditional maths publications, and I like the goals of the mathlib community e.g. "building a unified mathematical library".

David Ang said:

I've been contributing to mathlib(3) since 2022 so I'm not a new member, but my rationale is simply that I like clean code, I want to publish some of my code akin to traditional maths publications, and I like the goals of the mathlib community e.g. "building a unified mathematical library".

I agree with you, and this is my reason too, but for this new gen -- that reason would seem antithetical to how they are going about it.

Again, not trying to be mean, I just want to know their rationale for myself cause it seems to now be something entirely different to how I think tbh

As a new member, there is no obvious the pragmatic benefit and I found long 3k PR queue quite frustrated. I still enjoy playing Lean simply because for me modern advanced mathematics is so deep that I have to employ some 'non-linear' learning pattern: try at least to let pieces(concepts/theorems) make sense without checking every detail first and to see whether the pieces together combine to a meaningful framework, while playing Lean is quite at the opposite: it forces one to think calmly, understand every single piece thouroghly and find out the best route to write it down.

An example of 'non-linear' learning pattern: assume that a senior professor want to give a course on the representation theory of reductive groups without a fully robust introduction to "reductive groups" (I am sure it happens in reality). It is very likely that the first two lectures will begin like this: introduce the definition of reductive groups and things like (semi-simple, Borel, Levi), classifications, some basic properties without proofs accompanied with consistent examples from "GL_n", and finally provide references for the full generality and proofs together with a comfort "no worry if you don't understand everything because you will still learn a lot by just assuming the group is GL_n or your favourite split one". Then move on to the more representation theoretic part instead of spending two more lectures on the group theoretic part: look, we don't even have reductive groups in Mathlib.

There's a Tau Ceti roadmap for them though. I agree that it's a shame that there is no reductive group in mathlib but note that a reductive group is quite a complex object (a Lie group or a group scheme) and we've only recently been able to start saying nontrivial things about group schemes in mathlib

Kevin Buzzard said:

There's a Tau Ceti roadmap for them though. I agree that it's a shame that there is no reductive group in mathlib but note that a reductive group is quite a complex object (a Lie group or a group scheme) and we've only recently been able to start saying nontrivial things about group schemes in mathlib

Is it an on-going project or staying as roadmap? I agree it is highly intricate but it blocks so many fancy things e.g. Shimura varieties from being able to state. I would be very interested in it if there is such a project.
I wasn't particularly good as a researcher but I loved doing math and miss it.

Jiaxi Mo said:

Is it an on-going project or staying as roadmap? I agree it is highly intricate but it blocks so many fancy things e.g. Shimura varieties from being able to state. I would be very interested in it if there is such a project.

A Tau Ceti roadmap _is_ an ongoing (or a finished) project. Here is the roadmap, and you can see the theory being developed by AIs in directories in the actual Tau Ceti repo here.

@Jiaxi Mo Firstly , thanks so much for taking the time to reply ! I am sure it may have been intimidating as no one really new said anything , but that was very helpful( @Ryan Smith too , though a little bit more of a veteran here :stuck_out_tongue:).

I think perhaps you are thinking about addressing the gap between the math you do , roughly , and the full generality hieroglyphs of Mathlib. These genuinely take a very solid math maturity .

The good news , which is also the bad news , is the others are wanting to address the analogous gap for them — but for them it’s to get to research level maths that they see and use , vs for you it’s coursework based perhaps.

And as there is so much diversity there , as everyone wants that, this is also part of what almost necessitates going to these higher levels of generality , by default , in Mathlib .

I kind of can see the benefit of what you say and indeed some repos I’ll try find later (on phone) try bridge that coursework gap , at least with what is already reachable from the currently defined generality of Mathlib.

Oh and I guess it’s worth mentioning that the scale of this effort , also ends up needing a good amount of human code optimisation EVEN though Lean is not about coding internals.

Since all code you put in will need to be maintained in perpetuity , and Mathlib shouldn’t build too long , etc.

So full AI PRs are just actively unhelpful in most settings , being more true the more significant the math is .

However for practical and pragmatic purposes , it makes sense to keep that in own repo since it’s more narrow and doesn’t need these considerations . And you maintain it yourself , not strangers .

I know there are tools being built to automate some of this Mathlib optimisation, but I think over time this will just raise the bar of the initial scaffold , and many cases will still need a human thoughtful assessment .
